cues.text: Marshall has a rule. It is the rule in every textbook, and it is worth stating fairly, because for most of the last century it was simply what everybody believed.
Before the rule, two more costs. Both are averages — a total, shared out over every unit she makes.
Take everything she spends that moves with output — the wood, the power, the wages — and divide it by the number of chairs. That is her average variable cost.
average variable cost. What each extra chair costs her to make.
Now add a share of the cost of the building itself — the factory that had to be paid for before a single chair was made. Put those together and you have her long-run average cost.
long-run average cost. Everything a chair costs her, including a share of the building.
And now Marshall's rule, in two halves.
This is the most important picture in the film, so we build it slowly. One line, running up the screen. Low down means money coming in each month is poor. High up means it is good.
Marshall's first half. If the money coming in clears the long-run average cost — everything, including the building — then build. Expand. Enter the trade.
Marshall's second half. If the money coming in drops below the average variable cost — if a chair no longer covers even the wood and the wages — then stop. Shut down, or leave.
Notice how close together those two lines are. Between them there is a small band where the right thing to do is nothing at all. Hold that thought. That band is going to get very much wider.
One definition left, and it is the single most important one in this film. Take your time over it.
Nell needs a large sum to build. It comes from one of two places, and usually both.
She borrows it, and then she has to pay extra for the use of it.
Or it is her own money, and by putting it into this factory she gives up whatever else she could have done with it.
Either way, the money has a price. Blend the two together and you get one number.
The cost of capital. The yearly percentage the money she uses has to earn, just to be worth using at all.
Earn less than that, and she would have done better leaving the money where it was. That is the whole idea, and every number later in the film is measured against it.
AVC: what one more chair costs
LRAC: plus a share of the building
build above LRAC · shut below AVC
cost of capital: what money must earn
